brief.situation: 10:00 in a family practice. Mr. Petrov, 61, is here for a blood pressure follow-up. The medical assistant's reading is 194/123; he says he has 'a bit of a headache' and wants a refill.
handover: Hypertension on amlodipine 10 mg; type 2 diabetes on metformin; no anticoagulant. Last visit 136/84.
The office has a portable monitor and a glucometer; the nearest stroke center is 15 minutes away by ambulance.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Decide whether this is severe hypertension to manage here or an emergency to send out.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. The case ends 45 minutes in, then a debrief scores what you did.

cues.question: Is Mr. Petrov's blood pressure something to manage in the office or an emergency, and what decides it?

parts.label: What decides it
parts.criteria: Says that above 180/120 the question is acute target-organ damage; names the arm drift, facial droop and slurred speech as a focal neurological deficit (possible stroke), which makes it an emergency; glucose checked to exclude a mimic.
parts.modelAnswer: 194/123 alone is severe hypertension; without acute target-organ damage it is managed as an outpatient. His slurred speech, left facial droop and arm drift are a focal deficit, so this is a possible acute stroke and an emergency. A normal glucose rules out hypoglycemia as a mimic.

parts.label: What to do
parts.criteria: Calls 911 to a stroke center at once; fixes the time last known well (09:20) because treatment depends on it; gives no oral antihypertensive or aspirin in the office; hands off onset time, deficits, glucose and medications.
parts.modelAnswer: Call 911 for a suspected stroke now, establish last known well (09:20, confirmed by his wife), give nothing by mouth (no clonidine to chase the number, no aspirin before imaging), and hand off the onset time, the deficits, the glucose and his medications.

expertPath.text: Ask about new symptoms: slurred speech and a clumsy left hand since 09:20.
Focused neurological check: facial droop, arm drift, slurred speech. Fingerstick glucose 142.

denseDeficit.headline: A stroke progressed in the office
denseDeficit.body: Find when the neurological check happened and when 911 was called. The number on the cuff was not the question; the deficit was.

wentHome.headline: Sent home with a stroke
wentHome.body: Severe hypertension is outpatient only without acute organ damage. Asking about new symptoms and checking face, arm and speech would have found it.

strokeTarget.headline: Red flag found and referred
strokeTarget.body: A neurological check, 911 within minutes, last known well, glucose, no office drug and a full handoff. That is the expert path.

strokeLate.headline: Referred, by a slower route
strokeLate.body: He went, but check when the exam and the call happened, whether onset and glucose were known, whether a drug was given that the stroke team should decide on, and the handoff.

time_up.headline: Still in the office
time_up.body: A focal deficit with severe hypertension is an emergency referral.

scoring.modelReasoning: A reading of 194/123 is severe hypertension. The 2025 guideline manages severe hypertension WITHOUT acute target-organ damage as an outpatient, so the question is whether there is organ damage. His new slurred speech, left facial droop and arm drift are a focal neurological deficit: a possible acute stroke, which makes this an emergency referral. Check a glucose to exclude a mimic, establish last known well (treatment depends on it: thrombolysis within 4.5 hours), call 911 to a stroke center, give nothing by mouth (no oral agent to chase the number, no aspirin before imaging), and hand off onset time, deficits, glucose and medications.

bpQ.ask: His pressure is 194/123. Should you bring it down in the office before EMS arrives?

choices.label: Yes: give an oral agent now
No: with a stroke in progress, blood pressure is managed by the stroke team

bpQ.explain: Severe hypertension with acute target-organ damage is an emergency treated in hospital. In acute stroke, the blood pressure target depends on whether he gets thrombolysis (below 185/110 before it), which only the stroke team can decide after imaging.
